title: Comments and likes
like: the like counter under a post
brief: Under every post sits a like counter and a comment list. Millions tap the heart on the same famous post at the same moment. Showing the exact number is not essential, but showing the person their own like is.

clarify.q: Must the like count be exact?
clarify.a: No. A count that is a few seconds behind or off by a few is fine. It rounds to "1.2M" anyway.

clarify.q: Must I see my own like straight away?
clarify.a: Yes. If you tap the heart and it does not light up, you will tap again.
Comments should be kept. After a failure, at most the last 60 seconds of writes may need replay.

clarify.q: Do all posts get the same traffic?
clarify.a: No. One post may get 10 percent of all likes for an hour while a million others get none.

notes: A like is only a few bytes. The count is what people keep asking for.

Taps per second on the single hottest post

hints: What if one row in your database got 10,000 writes per second?
A cache in front handles repeat reads of the same count. A queue turns a burst of writes into a steady drip that workers apply in batches.
Try: app servers -> distributed cache -> key-value store for reads. For writes: app servers -> queue -> worker pool -> key-value store. Show the user their own like from the app, not from the cache.

editorial.summary: A like counter is a hot key in disguise. The fix is to stop treating each tap as a database write. Absorb the burst in a queue, add the taps up in workers, and serve the number from a cache. The database sees a few updates per second per post instead of thousands.

designs.name: Cache for reads, queue and batch for writes
designs.why: Reads of counts and comments come from a distributed cache. Likes go into a queue, and workers apply them in batches, so the hot post becomes a handful of updates per second. The key-value store stays comfortable even when the hottest post takes a tenth of all taps.

tradeoffs: A five-second cache keeps counts cheap but means a count can be five seconds old. Rounding to "1.2M" hides it.
Batching likes in workers saves the database but means a crash can lose the last few seconds of taps. That is the "lose up to a minute" trade the requirement allows.
Showing the user their own like from the app, and not from the cache, avoids the double tap at no cost.
Splitting a hot counter into several parts spreads the writes but makes the total a sum of parts.
editorial.realWorld: Counters for the most liked posts are commonly kept in memory and written to the database in batches of seconds (approx.). The same post can take well over 10,000 taps per second in a burst.

correctness.prompt: Comments and likes: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A measured replication or backup gap of at most 60 seconds, with a tested replay plan
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 7,500 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $36,064. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
